10.9. LIST COMPREHENSION 127
In many contexts, the diﬀerent kinds of sequences (strings, lists, and tuples) can
be used interchangeably. So how and why do you choose one over the others?
To start with the obvious, strings are more limited than other sequences becaus e
the elements have to be characters. They are also immutable. If you need the
ability to change the characters in a string (as opposed to creating a new string ),
you might want to use a list of characters instead.
Lists are more common than tuples, mostly because they are mutable. But there
are a few cases where you might prefer tuples:
1. In some contexts, like a return statement, it is syntactically simpler to create
a tuple than a list. In other contexts, you might prefer a list.
2. If you want to use a sequence as a dictionary key, you have to use an im-
mutable type like a tuple or string.
3. If you are passing a sequence as an argument to a function, using tuples
reduces the potential for unexpected behavior due to aliasing.
Because tuples are immutable, they don’t provide methods like sort and reverse,
which modify existing lists. However Python provides the built-in functions sorted

12.1 Hypertext Transfer Protocol - HTTP
The network protocol that powers the web is actually quite simple and there is
built-in support in Python called socket which makes it very easy to make network
connections and retrieve data over those sockets in a Python program.
A socket is much like a ﬁle, except that a single socket provides a two-way connec-
tion between two programs. You can both read from and write to the same s ocket.
If you write something to a socket, it is sent to the application at the other end
of the socket. If you read from the socket, you are given the data which the other
application has sent.
But if you try to read a socket 1 when the program on the other end of the socket
has not sent any data, you just sit and wait. If the programs on both ends of
the socket simply wai

lication has sent.
But if you try to read a socket 1 when the program on the other end of the socket
has not sent any data, you just sit and wait. If the programs on both ends of
the socket simply wait for some data without sending anything, they will wait for
a very long time, so an important part of programs that communicate over the
Internet is to have some sort of protocol.
A protocol is a set of precise rules that determine who is to go ﬁrst, what they are
to do, and then what the responses are to that message, and who sends next, and
so on. In a sense the two applications at either end of the socket are doing a dance
and making sure not to step on each other’s toes.
There are many documents that describe these network protocols. The Hypertext

12.6 Parsing HTML and scraping the web
One of the common uses of the urllib capability in Python is to scrape the web.
Web scraping is when we write a program that pretends to be a web browser and
retrieves pages, then examines the data in those pages looking for patterns.
As an example, a search engine such as Google will look at the source of one web
page and extract the links to other pages and retrieve those pages, extracting links ,
and so on. Using this technique, Google spiders its way through nearly all of the
pages on the web.
Google also uses the frequency of links from pages it ﬁnds to a particular page as
one measure of how “important” a page is and how high the page should appear
in its search results.

XML looks very similar to HTML, but XML is more structured than HTML. Her e

Each pair of opening (e.g., <person>) and closing tags (e.g., </person>) represents

Notation - JSON
The JSON format was inspired by the object and array format used in the
JavaScript language. But since Python was invented before JavaScript, Python’s
syntax for dictionaries and lists inﬂuenced the syntax of JSON. So the format of
JSON is nearly identical to a combination of Python lists and dictionaries.
Here is a JSON encoding that is roughly equivalent to the simple XML from above:
{
"name" : "Chuck",

to the “phone” tag. In JSON, we simply have key-value pairs. Also the XML
“person” tag is gone, replaced by a set of outer curly braces.
In general, JSON structures are simpler than XML because JSON has fewer ca-
pabilities than XML. But JSON has the advantage that it maps directly to some
combination of dictionaries and lists. And since nearly all programming langua ges
have something equivalent to Python’s dictionaries and lists, JSON is a very nat-
ural format to have two cooperating programs exchange data.
JSON is quickly becoming the format of choice for nearly all data exchange between
applications because of its relative simplicity compared to XML.

13.6 Application Programming Interfaces
We now have the ability to exchange data between applications using Hypertext
Transport Protocol (HTTP) and a way to represent complex data that we are send-

The next step is to begin to deﬁne and document “contracts” between applications
using these techniques. The general name for these application-to-application con-
tracts is Application Program Interfaces (APIs). When we use an API, generally
one program makes a set of services available for use by other applications and
publishes the APIs (i.e., the “rules”) that must be followed to access the services
provided by the program.

We see many examples of SOA when we use the web. We can go to a single web

maintain only one copy of data (this is particularly important for thing s like hotel
reservations where we do not want to over-commit) and (2) the owners of the data

13.7 Security and API usage
It is quite common that you need an API key to make use of a vendor’s API. The
general idea is that they want to know who is using their services and how much
each user is using. Perhaps they have free and pay tiers of their services or have a
policy that limits the number of requests that a single individual can make during
a particular time period.
Sometimes once you get your API key, you simply include the key as part of POST
data or perhaps as a parameter on the URL when calling the API.

Other times, the vendor wants increased assurance of the source of the requests
and so they expect you to send cryptographically signed messages using shared
keys and secrets. A very common technology that is used to sign requests over
the Internet is called OAuth. You can read more about the OAuth protocol at
www.oauth.net.
Thankfully there are a number of convenient and free OAuth libraries so you can
avoid writing an OAuth implementation from scratch by reading the speciﬁcat ion.
These libraries are of varying complexity and have varying degrees of richness. T he
OAuth web site has information about various OAuth libraries.

15.1 What is a database?
A database is a ﬁle that is organized for storing data. Most databases are organized
like a dictionary in the sense that they map from keys to values. The biggest
diﬀerence is that the database is on disk (or other permanent storage), so it pers ists
after the program ends. Because a database is stored on permanent storage, it can
store far more data than a dictionary, which is limited to the size of the m emory
in the computer.
Like a dictionary, database software is designed to keep the inserting and accessi ng
of data very fast, even for large amounts of data. Database software m aintains its
performance by building indexes as data is added to the database to allow the
computer to jump quickly to a particular entry.
There are many diﬀerent database systems which are used for a wide variety of pur-
poses including: Oracle, MySQL, Microsoft SQL Server, PostgreSQL, and SQLite.
We focus on SQLite in this book because it is a very common database and is
already built into Python. SQLite is designed to be embedded into other applica-
tions to provide database support within the application. For example, the Firef ox
browser a

15.14 Summary
This chapter has covered a lot of ground to give you an overview of the basics of
using a database in Python. It is more complicated to write the code to use a
database to store data than Python dictionaries or ﬂat ﬁles so there is little reason
to use a database unless your application truly needs the capabilities of a database.
The situations where a database can be quite useful are: (1) when your application
needs to make many small random updates within a large data set, (2) when your
data is so large it cannot ﬁt in a dictionary and you need to look up information
repeatedly, or (3) when you have a long-running process that you want to be able
to stop and restart and retain the data from one run to the next.

You can build a simple database with a single table to suit many application needs,
but most problems will require several tables and links/relationships between row s
in diﬀerent tables. When you start making links between tables, it is importa nt to
do some thoughtful design and follow the rules of database normalization to m ake
the best use of the database’s capabilities. Since the primary motivation for us ing
a database is that you have a large amount of data to deal with, it is impor tant to
model your data eﬃciently so your programs run as fast as possible.
15.15 Debugging
One common pattern when you are developing a Python program to connect to
an SQLite database will be to run a Python program and check the results using
the Database Browser for SQLite. The browser allows you to quickly check to see
if your program is working properly.
You must be careful because SQLite takes care to keep two programs from changing
the same data at the same time. For example, if you open a database in the brow ser
and make a change to the database and have not yet pressed the “save” button
in the browser, the browser “locks” the database ﬁle and kee

same time. For example, if you open a database in the brow ser
and make a change to the database and have not yet pressed the “save” button
in the browser, the browser “locks” the database ﬁle and keeps any other program
from accessing the ﬁle. In particular, your Python program will not be able to
access the ﬁle if it is locked.
So a solution is to make sure to either close the database browser or use the
File menu to close the database in the browser before you attempt to access the
database from Python to avoid the problem of your Python code failing because
the database is locked.

foreign key A numeric key that points to the primary key of a row in another

candidate as the logical key for the user’s data.

normalization Designing a data model so that no data is replicated. We store

using a foreign key.
primary key A numeric key assigned to each row that is used to refer to one row
in a table from another table. Often the database is conﬁgured to automati-

relation An area within a database that contains tuples and attributes. More
typically called a “table” .
tuple A single entry in a database table that is a set of attributes. More typicall y

The gmodel.py program handles a number of data cleaning tasks.
Domain names are truncated to two levels for .com, .org, .edu, and .net. Other
domain names are truncated to three levels. So si.umich.edu becomes umich.edu
and caret.cam.ac.uk becomes cam.ac.uk. Email addresses are also forced to lower
case, and some of the @gmane.org address like the following
arwhyte-63aXycvo3TyHXe+LvDLADg@public.gmane.org
are converted to the real address whenever there is a matching real email address
elsewhere in the message corpus.
In the mapping.sqlite database there are two tables that allow you to map both
domain names and individual email addresses that change over the lifetime of the
email list. For example, Steve Githens used the following email addresses as he
changed jobs over the life of the Sakai developer list:
s-githens@northwestern.edu
sgithens@cam.ac.uk
swgithen@mtu.edu
We can add two entries to the Mapping table in mapping.sqlite so gmodel.py will
map all three to one address:
s-githens@northwestern.edu -> swgithen@mtu.edu
sgithens@cam.ac.uk -> swgithen@mtu.edu

A.4 Preface for “Think Python”
A.4.1 The strange history of “Think Python”
(Allen B. Downey)
In January 1999 I was preparing to teach an introductory programming class in
Java. I had taught it three times and I was getting frustrated. The failure ra te in
the class was too high and, even for students who succeeded, the overall level of
achievement was too low.
One of the problems I saw was the books. They were too big, with too much
unnecessary detail about Java, and not enough high-level guidance about how to
program. And they all suﬀered from the trap door eﬀect: they would start out
easy, proceed gradually, and then somewhere around Chapter 5 the bottom would
fall out. The students would get too much new material, too fast, and I would
spend the rest of the semester picking up the pieces.
Two weeks be

y, and then somewhere around Chapter 5 the bottom would
fall out. The students would get too much new material, too fast, and I would
spend the rest of the semester picking up the pieces.
Two weeks before the ﬁrst day of classes, I decided to write my own book. My
goals were:
• Keep it short. It is better for students to read 10 pages than not read 50
pages.

A.4. PREF ACE FOR “THINK PYTHON” 219
• Be careful with vocabulary. I tried to minimize the jargon and deﬁne each
term at ﬁrst use.
• Build gradually. To avoid trap doors, I took the most diﬃcult topics and
split them into a series of small steps.
• Focus on programming, not the programming language. I included the min-
imum useful subset of Java and left out the rest.
I needed a title, so on a whim I chose How to Think Like a Computer Scientist .
My ﬁrst version was rough, but it worked. Students did the reading, and they
understood enough that I could spend class time on the hard topics, the interesting
topics and (most important) letting the students practice.
I released the book under the GNU Free Documentation License, which allows
users to copy, modify, and distribute the book.
What happened next is the cool part. Jeﬀ Elkner, a high school teacher in Vir-
ginia, adopted my book and translated it into Python. He sent me a copy of his
translation, and I had the unusual experience of learning Python by reading my
own book.
Jeﬀ and I revised the book, incorporated a case study by Chris Meyers, and in 200 1
we released How to Think Like a Computer Scientist: Learning with Python ,

Other books from Green Tea Press are available at greenteapress.com.
In 2003 I started teaching at Olin College and I got to teach Python for the ﬁrst
time. The contrast with Java was striking. Students struggled less, learned more,
worked on more interesting projects, and generally had a lot more fun.
Over the last ﬁve years I have continued to develop the book, correcting errors,
improving some of the examples and adding material, especially exercises. In 200 8
I started work on a major revision—at the same time, I was contacted by an editor
at Cambridge University Press who was interested in publishing the next edition.
Good timing!

FOREWORD 
Artificial Intelligence is entering a new era in which systems are no longer limited to generating predictions 
or assisting users with isolated tasks. Agentic AI represents this transformation by enabling intelligent 
systems to perceive their environments,  reason over complex objectives, plan multi -step actions, utilize 
external tools, collaborate with humans and other agents, and continuously adapt to changing conditions. As 
autonomous capabilities mature, Agentic AI is rapidly becoming one of the defining research and application 
areas of contemporary artificial intelligence. 
This edited volume, Agentic AI in the Age of Autonomy with Concepts and Case Studies, has been prepared 
to provide a comprehensive perspective on this emerging paradigm. Rather than focusing solely on technical 
advances, the book brings together interdisciplinary contributions that examine the architectural foundations 
of agentic systems, human -agent collaboration, governance, domain -specific applications, and future 
research directions. The diversity of the chapters reflects our belief that the future of autonomous AI will be 
shaped not only by technological innovation but also b

1. Introduction: From Intelligent Tools to Autonomous Agents
1.1. Background and Context 
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transitioning from assistive computational tools to autonomous, goal-directed, and interactive 
systems that can function in intricate socio -technical environments. Throughout history, AI applications have been 
primarily employed to facilitate human decisi on-making by means of data, pattern recognition, prediction, and 
recommendation [1]. The emergence of agentic AI systems has been facilitated by recent advancements in machine 
learning, natural language processing, reasoning with large language models, tool integration, and multi -agent 
coordination. These systems are capable of interpreting goals, planning actions, utilizing external tools, interacting with 
human users, and coordinating with other artificial agents  [2], [3] . This transition has resulted in agentic AI being a 
technically distinctive form of automation, as the system is capable of initiating intermediate decisions and operational 
actions in dynamic settings, in addition to producing outputs for  human evaluation.  Agentic AI systems ar

The interaction between humans and technology has been significantly altered by the emergence of agentic AI systems in 
socio-technical contexts. Autonomous systems are transitioning from pass ive instruments to active collaborators in 
decision-making. This transition necessitates a methodical comprehension of the methods by which humans and artificial 
agents can collaborate, allocate responsibilities, and mitigate risks. Therefore, the challeng e of human –agent 
collaboration is not limited to technical aspects; it also encompasses cognitive, organizational, and ethical challenges. A 
structured relationship in which human actors and artificial agents share decision authority, task responsibility, 
interpretive judgment, and operational control should be the way we conceptualize collaboration in agentic 
environments. This distribution is rarely unchanging; it is contingent upon the reversibility of potential outcomes, system 
maturity, user expertise,  task complexity, and domain risk. This section addresses the risks and constraints tha t are

monitoring routines. The results also have professional implications. Basic AI literacy is inadequate in agentic 
environments. A form of agentic AI literacy is required for professionals and administrators, which includes the following: 
levels of autonomy, memory functions, tool-use capacities, failure modes, signals of uncertainty, escalation procedures, 
and accountability pathways. Human oversight may be symbolic in the absence of such literacy, as users may not possess 
the knowledge or authority to query, interrupt, or correct agentic workflows. The primary conclusion is that responsible 
agentic AI necessitates calibrated autonomy. Autonomy should be expanded in situations where duties are well-defined, 
risks are manageable, outcomes are reversible, and monitoring mechanisms are reliable. It should be restricted in areas 
where there is a high degree of uncertainty, vulnerabili

or user-based validation. Its primary role is to integrate the technical and collaborative underpinnings of agentic AI and 
to establish a methodical framework for the operation of autonomous  agents in human -centered workflows. 
Consequently, the model that was developed in this chapter should be regarded as a conceptual foundation for future 
empirical research, rather than a validated explanatory model. The second constraint is the rapid advancement of agentic

1. Introduction: From Agentic Autonomy to Trust and Governance 
1.1. Background and Context  
The nexus of technological capability, human judgment, and institutional decision-making is profoundly altered by agentic 
artificial intelligence (AI) systems. In the past, AI applications have primarily benefited human actors by generating 
predictions, classifications, recommendations, or other analytical output for further evaluation [1]. Furthermore, agentic 
AI systems demonstrate varying degrees of adaptability, context reasoning, autonomy, goal -oriented behavior, tool use, 
and interaction with users or other artificial agents [2], [3]. They are capable of establishing objectives, coordinating 
actions, making intermediate decisions, and functioning in dynamic socio -technical environments. Consequently, their 
adoption cannot be merely attributed to technical performance. It is also contingent upon the comprehension, trust, 
supervision, contestation, and legitimization of autonomous behavior by human consumers, organizations, affected 
communities, and regulatory institu tions. The defining characteristics of agentic AI —adaptab

1.4. Scope of the Study 
The scope of this chapter is conceptual, analytical, and application-oriented. This chapter examines agentic AI systems as 
autonomous socio-technical systems that influence human judgment, organizational routines, institutional accountability, 
and public trust. The sole discussion of technical capabilities is in the context of their impact on perceived agency, trust,

prioritized.

automation anxiety, perceived control, and communication strategies. Secondly, the development of a conceptual model

2.2. Trust Formation in Agentic Contexts 
The acceptance and effective use of agentic AI systems are significantly influenced by trust. Trust formation in agentic 
contexts is a multifaceted process that is influence d by a variety of interrelated factors, such as transparency, perceived 
competence, and alignment with user objectives and values. Competence is the system's capacity to perform tasks with 
precision and dependability [18]. The empirical evidence indicates that user trust is primarily determined by  consistent 
performance and demonstrated accuracy, particularly in high -stakes application domains. However, the definition of 
competence in agentic AI should be more comprehensive than simply output accuracy. Additionally, it encompasses the

system's capa city to select suitable tools, maintain task continuity, identify ambiguity, prevent the inappropriate 
escalation of autonomy, and operate within domain -specific constraints. A system that excels in discrete tasks (e.g., 
question answering) may still be untrustworthy if it is unable to recognize its own limitations, perform multi-step actions, 
or prevent negative downstream consequences. Transparency is the degree to which the system's processes and decisions 
are visible and comprehensible to the consumers.  Transparency is also crucial for the establishment of trust [39]. 
Transparent systems enable the user to e valuate the rationale behind decisions, thereby enhancing confidence and 
reducing uncertainty. Nevertheless, the enhancement of the transparency of intricate AI models, particularly those that 
are built on deep learning architectures, is a significant obst acle [40]. In order to achieve this objective, interpretable 
interface design and explainable AI (XAI) are being utilized mor e frequently to offer users valuable insights into system

3. An Integrated Conceptual Model of Agentic AI Adoption 
As agentic AI systems become more prevalent, it is evident that a robust theoretical framework is required to elucidate 
the manner in which individuals and organizations assess, implement, and engage with these technologies. The 
Technology Acceptance Model  and Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology, which are currently in use, 
provide valuable insights; however, they are not entirely appropriate for addressing the distinctive characteristics of 
agentic systems, particularly their perceived agency, adaptability

agentic systems, particularly their perceived agency, adaptability, and autonomy. We require such a model because the 
adoption of agentic AI is not a simple matter of whether or not users find a system to be user -friendly or beneficial. On 
the other hand, the rate of adoption is contingent upon the extent to which users perceive the autonomy of the system,

Ecosystems 
The gradual development of independent socio-technical ecosystems, rather than the isolated refinement of individual AI 
tools, should be the perspective of the future evolution of agentic AI. Agents' influence will extend beyond individual tasks 
to organizational protocols, professional roles, governance structures, and social norms as they begin to plan, coordinate, 
communicate, and act across multiple systems. Therefore, the primary inquiry for future research and practice is how to 
reconcile the increasing autonomy of agentic systems with calibrated trust, human agency, institutional accountability,

and social legitimacy. The future should not be depict ed as a deterministic march toward complete autonomy. A more 
responsible approach is calibrated autonomy, which involves the selective and context -sensitive delegation of tasks to 
autonomous systems under conditions of transparency, human supervision, fair ness, auditability, and accountability. 
Autonomous socio -technical ecosystems will only be sustainable if they maintain meaningful human agency, protect 
vulnerable groups, and maintain institutional responsibility as technical capabilities increase.

6.3. Long-Term Societal Implications and Future Research Agenda

technical ecosystems i n which autonomous systems influence daily routines, public services, social structures, and 
organizational procedures. These advancements have significant societal implications, particularly in terms of the 
distribution of power, democratic accountability , institutional trust, and inequality. Agentic systems can perpetuate 
inequalities in access, representation, and control over decision -making processes when they are used unfairly or 
inadequately regulated. In contrast, these systems can improve coordinat ion, reduce administrative burdens, enhance 
the quality of services, and increase joint problem -solving capacity across sectors when they are well designed and 
governed.

1. Introduction 
Until recently, AI has mainly been integrated into software systems as a tool assisting narrowly defined, human-controlled 
tasks. These deployments often rely on carefully engineered prompts and continuous human supervision to achieve 
reliable outputs. Experience from production environment s suggests that prompt -dependent workflows become 
increasingly difficult to scale and hinder real -time decision -making in uncertain environments. Furthermore, the 
continuous human monitoring needed to guide model behavior increases architectural coupling a nd elevates long-term 
software maintenance costs. 
Moving from model -centric interfaces toward agent -centric architectures changes how software systems employ AI. 
Rather than functioning as an isolated, stateless service, an agentic component maintains oper ational context, monitors 
environmental signals, selects tools, and executes multi -step workflows. This approach supports complex repository 
operations such as code review, telemetry analysis, and technical debt mitigation. These operations depend on historical 
data and structural context l

operations such as code review, telemetry analysis, and technical debt mitigation. These operations depend on historical 
data and structural context like dependencies and team conventions. Transforming standalone language models into 
autonomous software agents enables AI capabilities to be integrated more effectively into large-scale software systems. 
This transition builds on prior research in intelligent agents and more recent advances in LLMs (Large Language Model). 
The idea of agents has long been studied in AI and distributed systems, including frameworks for rational action, planning, 
and interaction with environ ments [1]. Tool use and reasoning -action loops connect language models to external 
functions, APIs, and software environments, enabling agents to sense, decide, and act beyond text generation [2]. In 
parallel, multi-agent approaches explore coordination among specialized agents to solve complex tasks via decomposition 
and collaboration. As systematically categorized in recent literature, this collaborative division of labor replicates 
structured organizational architectures, allowing heterogeneous agents to

structured organizational architectures, allowing heterogeneous agents to  overcome the computational and reasoning 
bottlenecks of solitary models through coordinated communication and collective decision -making frameworks [16]. 
Recent studies in AI -assisted software engineering further demonstrate how these capabilities can be embedded into 
practical development workflows while maintaining governance and operational control. These include mechanisms such 
as guardrails, approval gates, and auditability, which improve reliability and controllability [3]. 
To guide this discussion, this chapter addresses four core research questions: 
RQ1: How do autonomous agents fundamentally differ from prompt -driven applications, conversational interfaces, 
and conventional software components 
RQ2: In what ways do dynamic planning, contextual memor y, tool execution, and orchestration layers affect system 
reliability and performance during scaling? 
RQ3: Which interaction patterns enable autonomous agents to optimize workflows within software development, IT

operations, and data analysis? 
RQ4: What systemic risks arise from agent autonomy, and which governance mechanisms can mitigate these risks in 
production environments? 
Integrating autonomous components into production workflows introduces distinct architectural dependencies that affect 
system maintainability. The viability of these components as software teammates depends on deliberate architectural 
choices rather than temporary prompt design. 
This chapter offers four main contributions to the field. It establishes a taxonomy for practitioners to clarify the operational 
boundaries between AI agents, conversational chatbots, workflow automation, and standard software services. To explain 
system design evolution, we present a structured six-layer agentic stack that spans perception, memory, reasoning, action,

2. The Evolution of Agentic Systems: From Symbolic Planning to LLM-Based Collaboration 
Research on AI agents has a long history in artificial intelligence and distributed systems. Classical definitions describe an 
agent as an entity that perceives its environment through sensors a nd acts upon that environment through effectors in 
pursuit of goals [1]. Multi -agent systems extend this view by studying how multiple autonomous entities coordinate, 
negotiate, compete, or collaborate in shared environments [2], [3]. These classical concepts continue to underpin modern 
agent architectures because the central questions are still related to autonomy, perception,

ete, or collaborate in shared environments [2], [3]. These classical concepts continue to underpin modern 
agent architectures because the central questions are still related to autonomy, perception, action, coordination, and 
rational decision-making. 
Recent advances in LLMs have changed the practical meaning of software agents. Instead of being limited to predefined 
rules or symbolic planning, LLM-based agents can interpret natural language goals, reason over contextual information, 
call external tools, and revise plans based on feedback. The ReAct framework showed that reasoning traces and external 
actions can be interleaved, allowing language models to solve tasks through both internal reasoning and environment 
interaction [4]. Schick et.al. demonstrated that language models can learn to use external tools such as calculators, search 
engines, and APIs, thereby extending their functional capability beyond text generation [5].

3. Demarcating AI Agents: Conceptual Boundaries and Distinctions 
The term AI agent is frequently conflated with chatbots, automation scripts, or microservices, yet each represents only a 
subset of agentic capability. An agent is neither a stateless API call nor a static, single-function component. While chatbots 
provide immediate prompt responses within limited context windows and microservices expose fixed operations, an AI 
agent actively maintains state, pursues high-level objectives, and dynamically adapts its workflow based on environmental 
feedback. In practice, three characteristics distinguish AI agents from conventional software components: 
• Goal Orientation: The capacity to autonomously decompose a defined objective into an actionable sequence 
of intermediate steps.

• Situational Awareness: The maintenance of persistent state, leveraging historical interactions and real -time 
environmental signals. 
• Action Capabi lity: The execution of tool invocations, system interactions, and distributed multi -agent 
collaboration.

architecture. As shown in Table 1, conversational chatbots remain bound to session-specific context paths, and workflow

realign its operational execution with the shifting requirements of the task context.

4. Architectural Taxonomy and Operational Layers of Autonomous Agents 
A practical agent architecture can be described through six layers. The memory layer stores short -term task context and 
long-term organizational or project knowledge. The perception layer collects signals from repositories, logs, user 
interactions, tickets, telemetry, and external systems. The reasoning and planning layer decompose goals into 
intermediate steps, selects strategies, and revises plans when new evidence appears. The action layer connects the agent 
to tools such as APIs, databases, CI/C D (Continuous Integration/Continuous Deployment) pipelines, issue trackers, test 
runners, and documentation systems. The orchestration layer coordinates multiple agents, resolves conflicts, and 
manages shared context. The governance layer constrains agent behavior through permissions, approval policies, audit 
logs, monitoring, and evaluation. The operational lifecycle relies on a decoupling of environmental signals from execution 
policies. Figure 1 outlines this structural distribution demonstrating how the governance layer acts as an inline boundary 
checking mechanism over th

The agent receives environmental signals through the perception layer, stores and retrieves context through memory, 
plans actions through a reasoning layer, executes tool calls through the action layer, coordinates with other agents through 
orchestration, and remains constrained by governance mechanisms. 
AI-agent architectures have progressed from single-agent, low-autonomy workflows toward richer designs with integrated 
planning, memory, and tool use. Planning helps identify intermediate steps, memory preserves longer-term context, and 
tool use enables agents to move from suggestion to action.

Multi-agent decomposition can improve coverage and specialization, but it can also increase c oordination risk. Practical 
mitigations include a clear contract for each agent role, a shared context schema with provenance, and an orchestrator 
that resolves conflicts using explicit priority rules rather than implicit prompt ordering. 
For maintainable deployments, the above controls should be linked to measurable outcomes. Example metrics include: 
action reversal rate (how often actions must be undone), tool failure rate, policy violation rate, time to detection for 
incidents, and human review load for gated actions. These metrics support iterative improvement and make the 
autonomy, trust, and control tradeoff explicit.

6. Discussion: Design Trade-Offs for Agentic Software Systems 
The transition from AI tools to AI teammates introduces several design trade-offs. Autonomy versus controllability remains 
the central engineering trade-off. Higher autonomy can reduce human workload, but it also increases the potential impact 
of incorrect actions. Therefore, agent systems should not only be evaluated according to the amount of automation they 
provide but also according to how safely they operate within predefined authority boundaries. 
Another important consideration concerns productivity and verification effort. Agents may accelerate code review, testing, 
and operational analysis, but their outputs still require validation. If an agent produces too many low-quality suggestions, 
the human verification burden may exceed the productivity gain. Thi s makes precision, prioritization, and explanation 
quality important evaluation criteria. 
Multi-agent specialization introduces additional coordination overhead. Multi-agent systems allow each agent to focus on 
a specific concern, such as testing, architec ture, or technical debt. However, specialization also re

on introduces additional coordination overhead. Multi-agent systems allow each agent to focus on 
a specific concern, such as testing, architec ture, or technical debt. However, specialization also requires orchestration. 
Without clear role definitions and shared context schemas, multi -agent systems may generate redundant, inconsistent, 
or conflicting outputs. 
Trust must be balanced against the ri sk of excessive reliance. Developers may gradually trust agents that provide useful 
recommendations, but excessive trust can become dangerous if users stop critically evaluating agent outputs. To prevent 
over-reliance, agent systems should expose confidenc e levels, evidence links, uncertainty statements, and clear 
boundaries of responsibility. 
Finally, software teams should distinguish between short-term productivity gains and long-term maintainability. An agent 
that focuses only on immediate task completion may miss architectural consequences or technical debt accumulation. For 
this reason, agentic systems in software engineering should include both task -level evaluation and long -term quality 
metrics.

7. Conclusion 
Autonomous AI agents represent a paradigm shift in software engineering, transitioning system architectures from passive 
model invocation to active, goal-oriented execution. Rather than treating these components as superficial chat interfaces 
or thin API wrappers, sustainable system design requires v iewing them as stateful software entities capable of context 
perception, persistent memory management, dynamic planning, and tool execution. 
The Software Quality Companion framework presented in this chapter demonstrates how such cooperative agentic 
networks can manage complex tasks, including automated code reviews, test-suite generation, architectural consistency 
checking, and technical debt monitoring. However, as this implementation illustrates, expanding agent autonomy without 
corresponding engineering boundaries introduces systemic operational risks. Establishing rigorous governance protocols 
(comprising explicit permissions, action gating, and continuous observability) remains a prerequisite for building reliable 
and trustworthy

ational risks. Establishing rigorous governance protocols 
(comprising explicit permissions, action gating, and continuous observability) remains a prerequisite for building reliable 
and trustworthy systems. 
As agentic te chnologies mature, their integration into production environments will ultimately depend on rigorous 
software engineering discipline rather than raw model capabilities. Future systems will require well -defined agent 
responsibilities together with practical  governance mechanisms. Appropriate authority boundaries, measurable 
evaluation criteria, and auditable execution logs will all contribute to trustworthy deployments.

1. Introduction  
The rapid advancements in artificial intelligence technologies in recent years are profoundly impacting the field of 
education, both theoretically and practically. Particularly with the widespread adoption of Large Language Model (LLM) 
based systems, which were made public at the end of 2022, AI has moved beyond being merely a research topic and has 
become a technology that has effectively entered classroom environments [1], [2]. At the heart of this transformation are 
AI agents-structures that go beyond passive information transfer, capable of interacting with the environment, planning, 
and using tools [3]. 
Market projections indicate rapid growth in AI -enabled educational technologies; however, such  forecasts should be 
interpreted cautiously because they vary substantially according to market definitions, forecasting methods, and 
commercial assumptions [4], [5]. 
LLM-based AI agents aim to over come the limitations of traditional language models by integrating memory, planning, 
tool use, and reflection components. Through these components, agents gain the capacity to automate comple

to over come the limitations of traditional language models by integrating memory, planning, 
tool use, and reflection components. Through these components, agents gain the capacity to automate complex training 
tasks such as grading, information retrieval, and adaptive content generation [6]. However, a significant gap is the lack of 
an integrated perspective among researchers and practitioners regarding how these systems are designed and evaluated 
[7] [8]. 
A review of the existing literature reveals that the vast majority of studies addressing the role of artificial intelligence in 
education focus on specific tools (ChatGPT, Copilot, etc.) or individual use cases. However, a comprehensive and 
systematic literature review that evaluates the architectural features, pedagogical opportunities, and associated risks of 
AI agents as a whole has not yet been sufficiently developed [9]. This study aims to fill this gap. Blending computer science 
and educational technologies from an interdisciplinary perspective, this article both defines AI agents from a software

2.5 Quality Assessment 
Studies included in the final sample underwent a three-dimensional evaluation process in terms of methodological quality

categories; additional skepticism was applied to preprints. Systematic reviews and meta -analyses were considered to 
have the highest level of evidence, while case studies and technical reports were accepted as supporting sources.

3.2. Historical Development of AI Agents in Education 
The use of artificial intelligence agents in education, contrary to popular belief, predates the emergence of generative AI 
by a considerable margin. This process can be examined within the framework of three main, successive periods. 
First period: Symbolic and rule -based systems (1966 –1990s). The sy mbol of this period is the ELIZA program, 
developed by Joseph Weizenbaum at MIT between 1964 and 1966. Based on the principles of pattern matching and rule-
based response generation, ELIZA, although not designed for educational purposes, is notable for bei ng the first system 
to question the limits of human-machine interaction [16]. In the years following ELIZA, Jaime Carbonell's SCHOLAR (1970)

5. Pedagogical Opportunities Offered by AI Agents in Education 
The contribution of AI agents to education holds the potential for a profound pedagogical transformation that goes beyond 
mere efficiency increases.  This section examines two of the most well -documented dimensions of this potential: 
personalized learning and adaptive content delivery, and real -time feedback and automated assessment mechanisms. 
Both areas are examined based on both theoretical justifications and empirical findings.

5.1. Personalized Learning and Adaptive Content  
In traditional classroom settings, it is practically impossible for a teacher to simultaneously deliver individually tailored  
content to dozens of students. AI agents offer con crete potential for overcoming this structural limitation. Adaptive 
learning systems dynamically adjust content difficulty, presentation order, and pedagogical strategy by analyzing student 
performance data, interaction patterns, and conceptual gaps in real time. [26]. 
Indeed, a recent systematic review encompassing 25 Scopus-indexed studies reports that all research published between 
2019 and 2024 shows that AI-powered personalized learning systems positively impact student achievement, motivation, 
and participation. These studies also document a rapid evolutionary transformation, ranging from early rule -based 
systems to sophisticated LLM -based agent platforms that combine natural language processing and machine learning 
components.

5.2. Instant Feedback and Automated Evaluation  
In learning, the timing of feedback is as crucial as its content. In traditional education, it can take days or even weeks for 
a student to receive their homework or exam results; this delay weakens motivation and reinforces conceptual errors. AI 
agents have the capacity t o eliminate these structural delays: they can provide contextually sensitive, targeted, and 
reasoned feedback to a student's response within milliseconds.

6.1. Digital Addiction:A Conceptual Framework 
Digital dependency on AI agents is conceptualized as a two -dimensional construct, going beyond a simple matter of tool 
preference or habit: tool dependency and cognitive dependency. Tool dependency refers to the student's functional 
reliance on AI for tasks such as note -taking, resource searching, or drafting; while cognitive dependency describes the 
student's tendency to delegate higher -level mental processes such as understanding,  reasoning, conceptualizing, and 
judging to AI instead of carrying them out themselves [27]. 
Cognitive miser theory strongly supports this distinction at a theoretical level. According to this theory, individuals 
systematically avoid deep cognitive processing when they have access to low -cost and high -efficiency tools like AI, and 
this gradually develops into a pattern called cognitive inertia . Social Cognitive Theory explains how this tendency is 
reinforced and normalized through widespread peer use and environmental pressures

6.2. The Erosion of Student Autonomy: Empirical Evidence 
This risk is not merely a theoretical concern, but is also confirmed by empirical findings. A mixed-methods study conducted 
with 248 undergraduate students at a universi ty in Zimbabwe found that 32.7% of participants exhibited addiction

A 2024 study by the Wharton School of Business reveals an even more striking picture: students who used ChatGPT as a 
study assistant performed worse on exams. This finding points to the paradoxical nature of A I dependency, suggesting 
that short-term productivity gains can hinder genuine learning in the long run: while students may perceive output quality 
as high, their independent problem-solving skills are actually weakening [29]. 
Studies on the AIDep-22 scale developed in China further clarify this mechanism. Students fail to notice a decline in their 
true critical thinking skills when they incorrectly attribute the high -quality output produced by AI to their own abilities. 
Cognitive psychology explains this phenomenon with the concept of schema weakening: when external agents constantly 
generate ideas and structures for specific tasks, the user's internal schemas related to these tasks lose power due to disuse

systems offering adaptive content have consistently reported increased student achievement and motivation, with 
differences of up to 28% in conceptual mastery in STEM contexts. On the other hand, findings regarding the risk of digital

8.2. Recommendations for Future Research  
The literature gaps revealed in this study offer a concrete roadmap for fut ure research. The following five directions are 
considered priorities for the advancement of the field: 
• Long-term impact studies: The effects of AI agent interventions on student development should be measured 
using longitudinal designs on a yearly or semester basis. 
• Geographic diversity: Contextual empirical studies should be conducted in regions with low representation 
levels, such as the Balkans, the Middle East, and Africa. 
• Interdisciplinary design standards: Mechanisms should be established for collabo ration between the 
computer science and education communities to develop common assessment frameworks and architectural 
standards. 
• Addiction management pedagogy: Evidence-based teaching strategies and curriculum design principles 
aimed at reducing the risk of digital addiction should be developed and tested in the classroom. 
• K-12 and vocational education contexts: To balance the existing literature, which is heavily focused on higher 
education, applied research shoul

1. Introduction 
The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence tools has placed K12 educational institutions at a critical 
inflection point. School administrators, teachers, and pol icymakers face a binary choice that is, in practice, a false 
dichotomy: prohibit AI to preserve academic integrity or permit it and risk unstructured, unsupervised use that may 
undermine learning outcomes. The reality is that AI is already present in the l ives of students, regardless of institutional 
policy, and the fundamental question is not whether AI will shape K12 education, but rather how [4, 5]. This chapter 
argues that neither outright prohibition nor unrestricted access represents a viable path. The answer lies in a principled, 
architecturally enforced model of supervised AI integration, one that preserves teacher authority while enabling students 
to engage meaningfully with AI-assisted learning. 
Agentic AI represents a paradigm shift from reactive,  single-turn conversational tools to autonomous, goal -directed 
systems capable of multistep reasoning, planning and action [1]. In educational contexts, such a shift carries profound 
implications. Unlike trad

n conversational tools to autonomous, goal -directed 
systems capable of multistep reasoning, planning and action [1]. In educational contexts, such a shift carries profound 
implications. Unlike traditional AI tools that respond to isolated querie s, agentic systems can guide students through 
iterative design cycles, provide contextual scaffolding, and interact with broader learning management infrastructures in 
ways that can either empower or bypass meaningful learning, depending on how these systems are governed [2, 3]. The 
stakes are particularly high in K12 environments, where learners are cognitively and ethically developing, teacher 
oversight is both pedagogically essential and legally mandated, and data privacy protections for minors impose st rict 
requirements on system architecture [7, 15], considerations that apply specifically to the K12 cohort in this deployment. 
SymDevAI Edu was designed and deployed in this context. SymDevAI Edu is a purpose -built agentic AI platform for K12 
education that operationalizes a closed-loop model of human-AI collaboration. At its core, the platform enables students 
to work alongside an AI agent to design, develop, and publish fun

2.1. Agentic AI: From Conversational Tools to Autonomous Agents 
The concept of agentic AI has emerged as a distinct research domain over the past several years, characterizing AI systems 
that go beyond single-turn question-and-answer interactions to exhibit autonomy, goal-directedness, multistep planning, 
persistent memory, and adaptive tool use [1, 3]. Kostopoulos et al. (2025) propose that for an AI system to be meaningfully 
classified as agentic, it must satisfy at least four of six core criteria: autonomy, multistep reasoning and planning, 
persistent memory, goal-oriented interaction, adaptive tool use, and contextual sensitivity [1]. This distinguishes agentic 
systems from conventional conversational agents that operate within isolated interaction sessions and lack continuity of 
purpose.

3.1. Conceptual Framework: Positioning Supervised Agentic AI on the Autonomy Spectrum 
AI systems deployed in educational settings can be positioned along a spectrum defined by two axes: the degree of AI

Framework: Positioning Supervised Agentic AI on the Autonomy Spectrum 
AI systems deployed in educational settings can be positioned along a spectrum defined by two axes: the degree of AI 
autonomy (the independence of the system) and the degree of human oversight (the  extent to which a teacher or 
institution controls outcomes). At one extreme sits the passive AI assistant, a tool that responds only when directly 
queried, produces no persistent artifacts, and requires the user to manually transfer outputs elsewhere. At the other 
extreme sits the fully autonomous educational agent, a system that sets its own learning objectives, generates and

103 
executes plans without human review, and interacts with learners without teacher mediation. Neither extreme is suitable 
for K12 deployment: the passive assistant fails to harness AI’s capacity for iterative, goal-directed support, while the fully 
autonomous agent displaces rather than supports teacher authority and raises unresolved ethical and safety concerns, 
particularly in child-facing K12 contexts [1, 7, 17]. 
SymDevAI Edu occupies a deliberate middle position on this spectrum, which we term supervised agentic AI. In this model, 
the AI system is genuinely agentic: it satisfies the criteria of goal -oriented interaction, multistep planning, adaptive tool 
use, and autonomous error repair [1, 3], but its agency is bounded at three structurally enforced checkpoints: (1) class 
enrollment requires explicit teacher approval; (2) all code and project artifacts remain on the student’s local d evice and 
are transmitted to the teacher only at the moment of assignment submission; and (3) no student work can be published 
or made visible beyond the classroom without both teacher nomination and administrator confirmation. These

This section presents the system architecture and pedagogical design of SymDevAI Edu. The platform is organized around

3.2. Client-Side Agentic Architecture: Design Rationale and Acknowledged Limitations 
The most distinctive feature of SymDevAI Edu is its client-side artificial intelligence (AI) execution model. Unlike dominant 
AI coding platforms, including Cursor AI, Google Antigravity, Claude Code, Replit, Lovable, and Qoder, which route all AI 
inference through centralized server-side API calls, SymDevAI Edu does not transmit student code or project content to its 
own servers. Instead, the AI agent operates entirely within the student’s local browser session, communicating directly 
with whichever public-facing AI chat interface the student has configured: Google Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude, DeepSeek, or 
any comparable web -accessible conversational AI system. The SymDevAI Edu backend servers store only lightweight 
metadata (user identifiers, project identifiers, LLM session references, and assignment linkages), but never the code, 
prompts, or project artifacts themselves. The student’s intellectual work remains on their own device throughout the

in K12 school environments. The AI interaction loop follows an incremental, conversational structure: the student 
formulates a prompt, either by typing or through a voice -to-text interface, which is relayed to the configured AI chat 
service. The AI agent returns the generated code or guidance, which the student reviews, tests, and optionally refines 
through further prompts. This prompt → generate → review → iterate cycle (the pedagogical core of the platform) 
positions the student as an active decision-maker who evaluates AI output rather than a passive recipient who accepts it.

5. Conclusion 
This chapter has presented SymDevAI Edu as a purpose-built supervised agentic AI ecosystem for K12 education, arguing 
that the binary framing dominant in educational policy discourse (prohibit AI or accept it uncritically) obscures a third and 
more pedagogically productive path: principled, architecturally governed integration. The platform addresses four of the 
most persistent challenges in AI-augmented K12 computing education simultaneously: the risk of cognitive offloading, the 
erosion of teacher authority, the cost barrier to institutional AI adoption, and the absence of authentic, audience -aware 
assessment for AI-assisted work. 
The platform’s most distinctive architectural feature is its client-side AI execution model, which decouples student learning 
activities from server -side inference costs. By routing AI interactions through students’ existing free -tier accounts on 
publicly accessible chat platforms rather than through platform -managed API calls, SymDevAI Edu achieves a cost 
structure that is genuinely accessible to K12 institutions operating under tight budget constraints.

a privacy dividend: student codes and project content never traverse the platform’s own servers, addressing the data 
sovereignty concerns that have deterred many institutions from adopting cloud-dependent AI tools [15, 17, 25]. The multi-
LLM configurability of the system further ensures that no institutional dependency on a single AI provider is created and 
that the platform remains functional as the AI service landscape continues to change. 
The pedagogical contributions of the platform center on two innovations: the timestamped prompt history as a mandatory 
assessment artifact and the SymDev Store as a quality -gated peer recognition system. The prompt log externalizes the 
cognitive process of AI collaboration, making it visible and directly assessable in K12 contexts. It transforms the question 
of assessment from “what did the student produce?” to “how effectively did the student direct the AI towards a purposeful 
outcome?”, a question that is far mo

https://symdevai.com/k12.html, and the full catalogue of teacher-approved student projects is openly browsable at the 
SymDev Store (https://symdevai.com/store-edu.html), providing a live demonstration of the computational artifacts K12 
learners can produce under supervised agentic AI guidance.

1. Introduction 
Tourism destinations are now managed under increasingly complex, multi -layered, volatile, and publicly scrutinized 
conditions. In previous years, destination management was often confined to promotion and visitor-attraction activities, 
while the need to co ntinuously balance economic value creation, environmental protection, residents’ well -being, 
infrastructure capacity, and long-term resilience remained insufficiently foregrounded [1, 2]. The OECD report shows that 
artificial intelligence is not merely a t ool for enhancing personalization or marketing performance in destinations; it can 
also support market intelligence, optimize visitor flows and traffic management through real-time data, and enable policy-
making based on more timely and granular evidence [3, 4]. 
The transformation enabled by artificial intelligence is particularly significant because many destinations now face a 
structural mismatch between the accelerating pace of tourism conditions and the slower operation of conventional 
reporting systems. Periodic reports, static indicators, and fragmented datasets are often in

ural mismatch between the accelerating pace of tourism conditions and the slower operation of conventional 
reporting systems. Periodic reports, static indicators, and fragmented datasets are often inadequate for understanding 
rapidly evolving pressures such as crowding, mobility, social sentiment, environmental stress, and seasonal fluctuations 
in demand [6]. As tourism destinations become more complex, dynamic, and multi-stakeholder systems, agentic AI offers 
a decision-support logic that can integrate diverse destination data, generate situational awareness, and support timely, 
human-supervised managerial responses. Destination management is therefore moving from retrospective reporting 
toward a more agile and evidence -based governance model that asks not only “what happened?” but also “what is 
happening, what may happen, and how should we intervene?” . In this respect, agentic AI offers an important decision -
support logic for managing the delicate balance among economic benefits, environmental protection, visitor experience, 
and local quality of life in destinations.

2. Conceptual Foundations of Agentic AI: From Traditional Artificial Intelligence to Agentic 
AI 
Artificial intelligence has evolved from systems that perform narrowly defined analytical tasks towards more autonomous, 
goal-oriented architectures with capacitie s for action [13]. In its traditional form, AI is generally used to classify data, 
recognise patterns, make predictions, automate repetitive tasks, or support human decisions within predefined 
boundaries [14]. Such systems are valuable because they can process large volumes of data faster than humans; however, 
they often operate as task-oriented tools that depend on explicit prompts, structured inputs, and human intervention to 
interpret outputs [15]. The emergence of agentic AI represents a major break in this development trajectory. Agentic AI 
refers to artificial intelligence systems organized around agents or multi -agent architectures that posse

emergence of agentic AI represents a major break in this development trajectory. Agentic AI 
refers to artificial intelligence systems organized around agents or multi -agent architectures that possess autonomy, 
intentionality, and the capacity for goal-directed behavior [16]. 
The transition from traditional AI to agentic AI is not only a technological development but also a conceptual shift in how 
intelligence is organised and applied [16]. Whereas traditional AI generally produces an output in response to a specific 
input, agentic AI structures the process a round perception, reasoning, planning, coordination, and action [16]. In this 
model, intelligence does not reside solely in a single algorithm; it emerges through the interaction of agents, data sources, 
tools, and feedback mechanisms. An agent may be understood as an autonomous entity that perceives its environment, 
evaluates information, makes decisions, and acts to achieve specific goals [17,18]. Multi -agent systems, in turn, are 
structures in which multiple agents cooperate, coordin ate, and communicate to solve problems in distributed 
environments [18-20]. This transformation also changes the role of AI in org

structures in which multiple agents cooperate, coordin ate, and communicate to solve problems in distributed 
environments [18-20]. This transformation also changes the role of AI in organizational and operational contexts [18]. 
Traditional AI primarily supports analysis; agentic AI extends this capacity toward adaptive and goal-oriented action [19]. 
Traditional AI identifies patterns, whereas agentic AI may use these patterns to plan subsequent steps [19]. Traditional AI 
assists human decision makers, whereas agentic AI can coordinate tasks within defined bound aries, interact with other 
agents, and generate context-sensitive responses [20, 21]. 
Agentic systems can operate across multiple knowledge bases, coordinate with peer agents, interpret changing conditions, 
and support real-time, data-driven decisions [16]. Nevertheless, the concept of agentic AI must be used carefully. A single 
universal definition of the term has not yet emerged in the literature [22]. Therefore, agentic AI is best understood as a 
family of architectures and methods based on agent -based r easoning, multi -agent coordination, and distributed 
interaction [16,22]. Its performance and

feedback, and adaptive decision-making capacities [14,16].

2.1. What Is Agentic AI? 
Agentic artificial intelligence is an AI approach composed of agents that perceive their environment, evaluate data, make 
decisions, and act on those decisions in order to achieve a specific goal [7,13,14,16,20]. Here, an agent is an intelligent 
unit capable of acting independently. It collects data, interprets the situation, compares options, selects the appropriate 
action, and monitors the outcome. In structures where multiple agents work together. The conceptual basis of agentic AI 
is rooted especially in the literature on multi -agent systems [7,13,14,16,20, 22]. Agentic AI is also closely related to the 
distributed AI approach [23].  
One of the most important advantages of agentic AI is that it provides flexibility, scalability, and resilience. In multi-agent 
systems, agents can be added, removed, or reconfigured [22]. This enables the system to adapt more easily to changing 
task requirements and environmental conditions. A distributed architecture can prevent the collapse of the entire system 
in the face of partial system failures, because local decision -making, inter-agent collaboration, and task sharing support 
sys

distributed architecture can prevent the collapse of the entire system 
in the face of partial system failures, because local decision -making, inter-agent collaboration, and task sharing support 
system continuity [23]. 
Another important dimension of agentic AI is its ability to support real -time decision-making in complex and dyn amic 
contexts [24]. Agents can produce decisions based on specific knowledge bases and environmental inputs; when 
necessary, they can co -ordinate with other agents to reach more integrated outcomes. Therefore, agentic AI should be 
understood not merely as an analytical tool but as a system that supports and monitors decision processes and, when 
needed, provides intervention capacity in the face of changing conditions. Agentic AI represents the evolution of artificial 
intelligence from a passive tool for ana lysis or content generation towards autonomous, goal -oriented, distributed, and 
coordinated decision-support systems [15]. At the core of the concept lies the ability of agents to perceive the 
environment, make decisions according to goals, communicate with other agents, and solve complex problems in a 
distributed manner [16].

• Stage 3: Data sources and the knowledge infrastructure must be established. For agentic AI to make decisions, 
it must have access to reliable, up -to-date, and meaningful data. These data may come from structured 
databases, sensors, digital platforms, user inputs, texts, images, reports, or external systems. 
• Stage 4: The tools that agents can use must be specified. Agentic AI systems are not merely analytical structures; 
when necessary, they perform operations by using digital tools. Database querying, calculation, reporting, file 
reading, web search, software-interface use, automatic notification generation, or initiating a specific workflow 
may be among these tools. 
• Stage 5: The decision -action loop must be designed. In agentic AI systems, the process generally proceeds

creating a plan, recommending or implementing action, monitoring the outcome, and revising the decision

• Stage 6: Human oversight and et hical boundaries must be defined. Because agentic AI possesses autonomous

Which decisions the system can make automatically, which decisions require human approval, and under which

• Stage 7: The system must be tested through a small-scale pilot application. Agentic AI is generally not established

Agentic AI structures the decision -support process through five basic stages: perception, interpretation, planning,

Situational awareness is the capacity to understand what is happening in a  particular environment, why it matters, and 
what it may imply for future action. In destination management, this capacity means monitoring current conditions, 
identifying emerging pressures, seeing the relationships among different indicators, and supporting timely decisions. For 
example, an increase in accommodation demand may be interpreted by itself as a positive economic signal. However, if 
traffic congestion, trail crowding, wildlife incidents, or negative community sentiment also increase during the same 
period, this may point to broader destination pressure. Similarly, visitor satisfaction becomes more meaningful when 
interpreted together with price, parking opportunities, responsible visitation messages, and perceptions of sustainability.

The practical contribution of this case is that it shows DMOs and local authorities that intelligent destination management 
is possible not merely by installing technology but by developing new organizational and governance capacities. DMOs 
need to be repositioned not only as promotional institutions but also as data coordinators, sustainability facilitators, and 
decision-support actors. Local authorities must be able to connect tourism data with infrastructure, transportation, land 
use, environmental protection, public safety, and community well -being. Data governance plays a critical role in this 
process: which indicators will be monitored, who will provide the data, how often the data will be updated, how data 
quality will be controlled, who will access the results, and how findings will be transformed into decisions must be clearly 
defined. Otherwise, dashboards may become visually powerful tools with limited managerial impact.

The transfer of agentic AI into destination management also entails important ethical and institutional risks. Decisions 
concerning visitor limits, environmental protection, mobility management, demarketing, spatial routing, and community 
priorities involve public values, social trade-offs, and political responsibilities, and therefore cannot be fully automated. 
Low-quality data may produce misleading recommendations, excessive  reliance on dashboards may reduce complex

management should therefore be designed within an input -processing-interpretation-recommendation-human 
approval-implementation loop. In such a model, the system collects information from multiple data sources, processes 
patterns, interprets them in relation to sustainability and local well -being goals, and produces prioritized 
recommendations; however, the final decision remains dependent on the ethical, political, and managerial judgment of 
human actors.

Although agentic AI offers significant potential for tourism governance, its practical adoption is constrained by several 
institutional, technical, and  financial limitations. The first limitation concerns institutional readiness. Many destination 
management organizations and local authorities still operate through fragmented administrative structures, limited digital 
expertise, and project -based decision -making routines. In such contexts, agentic AI adoption requires more than 
technological investment; it also requires organizational learning, inter-institutional coordination, staff training, and clear 
governance protocols. 
A second limitation concerns data interoperability. Agentic destination-management systems depend on the integration 
of heterogeneous data sources, including visitor flows, accommodation performance, mobility patterns, environmental 
indicators, resident sentiment, and public -service cap acity. However, these data are often collected by different 
institutions, stored in incompatible formats, updated at different intervals, and governed by different access rules.

Without common data standards, ethical data -sharing agreements, and reliable p ublic–private collaboration

Third, implementation costs may create inequalities between large, digitally mature destinations and smaller destinations 
with limited financial and human resources. Smaller destinations may struggle to invest in advanced data infrastructure, 
AI expertise, cybersecurity, software maintenance, staff training, and continuous system evaluation. Therefore, agentic AI 
should not be understood as a purely technical solution. Rather, it should be approached as a gradual governance 
transformation that requires scalable infrastructure, capacity building, human oversight, and context -sensitive 
implementation strategies.

6. Conclusion 
This chapter has shown that contemporary destination management increasingly requires smarter, more integrated, and 
more agile governance systems . Contemporary destinations are complex systems shaped by visitor mobility, 
infrastructure capacity, environmental pressure, resident well-being, digital reputation, climate risks, and changing travel 
behaviour. Under these conditions, traditional management tools based on periodic reporting, promotional planning, or 
fragmented institutional data are insufficient. Destination management must therefore turn towards systems that not only 
collect data but also integrate and interpret them, make early signals visible, and provide timely decision support.  
The main contribution of this chapter is that it establishes a conceptual bridge between agentic AI and destination 
management. Agentic AI refers to the transformation of artificial intelligence from a mere out put-generating tool into a 
more active structure that supports decision processes through autonomy, goal-oriented behaviour, percept

more active structure that supports decision processes through autonomy, goal-oriented behaviour, perception, planning, 
tool use, coordination, and adaptive response capacity.

Prompt design plays a critical role in the diagnostic performance of large language models in medical imaging tasks. In 
this study, different prompting strategies were implicitly ex plored, including single -step prompts and role -based 
instructions such as framing the model as a radiologist. The results suggest that structured prompts improve clarity and 
consistency in responses, while role -based prompting enhances domain -specific reasoning. However, the absence of

7.2.1 Prompt-Dependent Inconsistency 
One of the most striking findings of this study is the inconsistency of the model when analyzing the same image under 
different prompting conditions. In the first experiment, the model correctly identified bacterial pneumonia from a single 
X-ray image. However, when the same image was evaluated independently under a role -based prompt in a later 
experiment, the model failed to detect the infection and instead focused on an unrelated feature (clavicle fracture). This 
inconsistency highlights the strong dependence of diagnostic outcomes on prompt design and interaction context, 
suggesting that current multimodal AI systems lack stability and robustness in clinical interpretation tasks.

models to perform poorly. In the healthcare field, this situation can have serious consequences. For example, if the data 
does not fully reflect the general population in terms of characteristics such as certain ethnic groups, gender and age 
groups, it can produce incorrect results, which can lead to misdiagnosis. Accountability and trust should be at the highest

12. Conclusion 
The implementation of ChatGPT with images has some positive aspects. We asked ChatGPT to examine the test images in 
the dataset we used in the study. ChatGPT first shared the information on which criteria it conducted the review, and then 
shared the possible results. It even took the process a little further and advised the person. This provides preliminary 
evidence that ChatGPT can play an active role in medical image processing and can be used as a decision support system 
for doctors. However, giv en the limited sample size and observed inconsistencies, these findings should be interpreted 
with caution. Despite all these points, we see that ChatGPT-4o has serious problems in making correct predictions in the 
process of examining and evaluating Chest X-ray images. The success rate is very low. Therefore, it does not seem possible 
to use it in its current form for making a final diagnosis. Instead, it can be used to support doctors in performing analyses.

13. Future Directions in AI Diagnostics 
GPT-4 and similar models could evolve to analyze video feeds from procedures like endoscopy or ultrasound, providing 
clinicians with real-time insights. Combining imaging data with patient histories, lab results, and genetic information could 
lead to highly personalized diagnoses and treatment plans. With AI-powered diagnostic tools, remote healthcare facilities 
could provide expert-level analysis without requiring a physical presence, reducing geographic barriers to care. Future AI 
systems could implement continuous learning, allowing them to adapt to new medical knowledge and datasets without 
requiring complete retraining.
