1. Introduction 
1.1 The Rise of Agentic Commerce in 2026 
Not long ago, managers asked employees how they used chatbots, and the question was mostly about output safety. 
Chatbots are passive. They can recommend a product but will not act on it. The question now is different. Managers ask 
how people govern operative entities. An operative entity is a software agent that reads a client transcript, decides on a 
trade, routes the order, files the confirma tion, and eventually books the position. No human sits on the trade path 
anymore [1]. 
This shift is visible in the multi -agent systems deployed across production systems [2], in the convergence on tool -use 
protocols and orchestration frameworks [3], and in a growing body of work that treats the LLM as one component within 
a system rather than the system itself [P1]. 
Wealth management is one of the early adopters of this pattern and also one of the harder cases. The early adoption is 
because a junior advisor ’s day naturally breaks into narrow jobs, namely reading the request, pulling the constraints, 
drafting the order, routing the trade, and writing the audit trail, and each maps to an agent without much pai

naturally breaks into narrow jobs, namely reading the request, pulling the constraints, 
drafting the order, routing the trade, and writing the audit trail, and each maps to an agent without much pain. The hard 
part is regulatory. Every trade touches at least three regulators in the United States alone (FINRA, SEC, and IRS), and each 
regulator has its own definition of what an action is and who is on the hook when something goes wrong. The same recurs 
across jurisdictions. For example, suitability and  best-interest duties appear under MiFID II in the European Union and 
under the FCA Consumer Duty in the United Kingdom. The supervisory requirement we describe is not specific to one 
regulator. 
Regulatory inquiry has grown with deployment [1]. Software agents do not fail the way chatbots fail. They can act, and 
they are trained to follow instructions. That combination produces the problem we address next, the supervisory gap. 
1.2 The Supervisory Gap 
The supervisory gap is the regulator-side view of this problem. It names the gap between what an LLM-based agent claims 
to have verified and what the agent actually verified. The 2026 FINRA Report names several agent -specific

egulator-side view of this problem. It names the gap between what an LLM-based agent claims 
to have verified and what the agent actually verified. The 2026 FINRA Report names several agent -specific risks, four of 
which open this gap, namely autonomy without validation, action beyond  intended scope, non-transparent multi-step 
reasoning, and unintended exposure of sensitive data [1]. This chapter focuses on the first three. They produce a problem 
we call hallucinated compliance. Hallucinated compliance is what happens when an LLM -based agent, faced with a client 
instruction that conflicts with a rule, produces output that looks like it satisfies both but does not. 
Hallucinated compliance is not hallucination in the usual sense. The agent is not inventing facts. It is doing exactly what it 
was trained to do, which is to follow instructions. That trained objective works against what a regulator needs, which is 
for the agent to hold the line even when a request is intentionally framed to get around it. When the two conflict, the 
agent tends to produce a fluent rationalization. It says the constraint does not apply, or the client’s instruction waives it,

1.3 Explainability as a Supervisory Requirement 
Closing the supervisory gap is necessary but not enough. The 2026 FINRA Report raises auditability and transparency as a 
third concern, because multi-step agent reasoning can make outcomes hard to trace and explain [1]. Getting one decision 
right is only part of the job. The supervisor must be able to see why it was right. 
The financial-XAI literature reaches a similar position. A recent review finds that the core barrier to deployment is not the 
lack of explanation but the lack of explanations that are deterministic for the same input [5]. Post-hoc neural attribution

2. Literature Review 
2.1 Multi-Agent Architectures 
Multi-agent LLM systems in production are recent, but the theory behind them is not. Guo et al. provide the most thorough 
current survey of LLM-based multi-agent systems [2]. The role that matters most to our work is the Auditor or Critic, which 
appears across many domains. AutoGen is one of the earliest production-grade frameworks for composing such roles. It 
lets developers build agents that talk to each other, call tools, and ask human users for input [7]. Li et al. complement this 
with a survey of operational concerns at scale, covering stable inter-agent interfaces and the cost of redundant reasoning 
between agents [3]. 
Dual-agent designs help because they split labor between two kinds of agent. A single instructi on-following LLM will, in 
the limit, put the instruction ahead of the constraint, because that is what it was trained to do. Pairing it with a second 
agent, one that owns the constraint and is deterministic rather than generative, interrupts that conflict. The constraint no 
longer has to win inside one model’s objective, because it is enforced from outside the model.

2.4 GraphRAG and the Limits of Vector Retrieval for Regulatory Texts 
The retrieval-augmented generation literature has matured fast. Fan et al. offer the broadest current treatment of RAG in 
the LLM era, surveying retrieval strategies and integrat ion patterns that have worked in production [14]. Peng et 
al. present the first comprehensive survey of GraphRAG and make the case for graph structure in the retriever’s index 
[15]. Huang et al. characterize the conditions under which RAG keeps producing hallucinated outputs even when retrieval 
is grounded [16]. 
The case for graph structure in regulatory compliance is strong. Regulations refer to other regulations. A retrieval system 
based on vector similarity will surface FINRA Rule 2111 (Suitability) when the query mentions suitability. But it will not, in 
general, surface SEC Rule 144 (Restricted Securities) when 2111 has been triggered. The two are linked through restricted-
stock disposition logic that the semantic chunks themselves do not state. One solution is a graph index that encodes those 
references explicitly. ComplianceNLP is one such system. It generates a regulatory knowledge graph spanning the SEC,

Safety frameworks for LLMs in production come from two communities. One builds open-source toolkits, of which NeMo

[21]. The other develops governance frameworks for high-stakes domains. Shvetsova et al. give an architectural template 
for safety filtering in financial decision support, with explicit attention to real-time constraints and bidirectional validation 
[22]. Both share a structural feature. The safety component is outside the LLM and treats it as a candidate generator

Where these frameworks fall short for financial compliance is i n their model of policy. NeMo Guardrails encodes safety 
rules as Colang programs interpreted at runtime. Shvetsova et al.  similarly use rule-based filters. Neither is designed to 
express the conditional, evidence-dependent structure of a financial rule such as FINRA suitability. Such a rule evaluates 
differently depending on the client’s risk tolerance, prior loss history, and the volatility of the proposed instrument. Our 
deterministic auditor in §3 addresses this gap. It encodes rules as evaluable AST nod es with typed conditions, KYC 
predicates, and fallback evidence requirements. 
The wider literature confirms that compliance is the major concern in adoption. Singh et al., in a systematic review of 157 
articles on AI in banking and finance, count regulator y demands and a lack of transparency among the barriers to AI 
adoption [23]. Černevičienė and Kabašinskas reach the same conclusion from the explainability side [24]. Our 
architectural choices in §3 follow directly from both points.

3.3 Regulatory Knowledge Representation 
The Auditor’s deterministic behavior is grounded in a regulatory abstract syntax tree, or AST. The AST is loaded once at 
startup from a relational store of rule records, then cached for the process lifetime. A separate flat JSON corpus is served 
to the Proposer by a vector index for retrieval-augmented context on revision cycles. The two carry the same information 
for different purposes. The AST is the compiled form the rule engine evaluate s. The JSON corpus is the natural -language 
source the Proposer reads when the Auditor returns a RECOVERABLE failure and needs to know what evidence to seek.

The AST schema is intentionally narrow. Each Regulation carries an identifier, a Severity of CRITICAL or RECOVERABLE, and 
one or more RuleClause children. Each clause has a TriggerCondition (matching against the proposal action, asset ticker, 
or a prompt signal) and one or more KYCRequirement nodes that are evaluated when the trigger fires. A failed 
KYCRequirement may carry an optional EvidenceFallback. The presence of a fallback is what distinguishes a curable 
RECOVERABLE violation from a CRITICAL block. Listing 2 shows the schema by example. 
Our reference implementation covers eight regulations spannin g FINRA, the SEC, and the IRS. Table 2 lists each rule, its 
severity, and its institutional weight. Five rules are CRITICAL and act as binary gates: any triggered violation routes the 
trade to human escalation regardless of evidence. The other three are RE COVERABLE and can be cured by evidence 
through the continuous risk score.

3.4 Signal Detection: From Prompt to Triggered Rules 
The Auditor starts each evaluation by turning the cleaned user prompt into a set of regulatory signal tags. Algorithm 2 
summarizes the procedure. The EMBED procedure encodes the prompt both as full text and as sentence-split chunks. This 
catches violations buried in subordinate clauses that a single full-prompt embedding would smooth over. 
Embeddings come from an ensemble of two sentence-transformer models. The first is mukaj/fin-mpnet-base, trained on 
financial-domain text. The second is philschmid/bge -base-financial-matryoshka, a matryoshka -variant retrieval model 
also fine-tuned on financial corpora. Reimers and Gurevych [20] established the methodology for this class of models. 
We take the unweighted mean of the two models’ cosine similarities. That ensemble score is the basis for every 
downstream signal decision.

The embeddings then run against two checks, in the following order. First is the blacklist check. It compares each signal

The whitelist check runs only when the blacklist finds nothing. The ordering is deliberate. Innocent until proven suspicious.

KYC and AML verification, buying power, and po st-trade concentration. The concentration check is RECOVERABLE. Its 
fallback identifier is EVID_CONCENTRATION_ACK. The SBC formula can soften the violation when the client acknowledges 
the concentration risk.

3.6 Evidence Coverage via Ensemble Embeddings 
When the Auditor reaches a RECOVERABLE failure, the next question is whether the Proposer already supplied evidence 
that satisfies the requirement. The system computes a continuous evidence -coverage score 𝐶𝑒𝑣,𝑖 ∈ [0,1] for each 
missing identifier. Algorithm 4 summarizes the computation. Three choices in the algorithm are worth discussing. 
The first choice is the prompt -grounding check, the USABLE predicate. The Auditor r efuses any evidence scrap that does 
not appear verbatim in the client prompt. Without this anti -hallucination guard, a determined Proposer could attach a 
fabricated scrap and slip past the rule. 
The second choice is the affirmative-acknowledgment fast-path, the AFFIRMATIVE predicate. Fallback descriptions in the 
AST are long-form legal phrasings, while client responses are often a one -token “Yes” or “I understand.” The ensemble 
similarity between the two is predictably low, usually below 0.30. The fast -path resolves this. An acknowledgment 
requirement is about consent, not about matching phrasing.

After the gate decision is computed, control returns to the router, which routes on the gate decision and the proposed 
action. AUTO_APPROVE terminates the loop and commits the trade. HUMAN_ESCALATION terminates the loop and blocks 
the trade. Both write the ConstraintDelta to the audit trail. REFINEMENT passes the ConstraintDel

The orchestrator enforces a hard upper bound MAX_ITERATIONS on the number of refinement rounds. When the bound 
is reached without AUTO_APPROVE, the router escalates to human review regardless of the current risk score. The bound 
is intentionally small: it exists to stop a determined attacker from looping indefinitely against an Auditor that refuses to 
relax. The safety valve guarantees that escalation, not coercion, is the last resort.

4.5 Limitations and Honest Findings 
This evaluation has three limitations. 
The two weakest detection classes are SEC 10b -5 and SEC Regulation Best Interest, both at 83.8%. Each describes its 
violation indirectly, through who supplied a tip or how an order is routed rather than through an explicit illegal action. A 
system that claims reliable detection should report these honestly rather than average them away. The cascade map still 
recovers some of these cases at evaluation time, because firing a sibling rule pulls the weak clause into a forced evaluation. 
The recall gain came with a higher false -positive rate, near 10% on the normal -prompt corpus. We chose the floor that 
sits on a favorable point of this trade-off rather than the one that maximizes recall outright, because a compliance system

pays for false blocks in advisor friction. The right operating point is institution-specific, and the framework exposes it as a 
tunable parameter rather than fixing it. 
The legal control set in the supervised loop is small at 8 prompts. The 0% regulatory false-positive rate is encouraging, but 
the confidence interval at this size is wide. The 105-prompt legal set in the detection corpus gives a more stable estimate, 
and future runs should drive the full loop over a control set of the same or larger size. 
5. Conclusion 
Agentic finance should not require trusting an LLM to police itself. The architecture in this chapter splits two jobs into two 
different components. The first generates trade intent aligned with the client. The  second verifies that intent against 
codified rules. The two components do not fail in the same ways, and neither one alone is enough. Together they produce 
decisions that are both responsive and defensible. 
The Stochastic Boundary Control formulation make s the separation precise. The composite score 𝑅 is a transparent 
function over institutional inputs; its value at any routing

The Stochastic Boundary Control formulation make s the separation precise. The composite score 𝑅 is a transparent 
function over institutional inputs; its value at any routing decision can be reconstructed from a single log line. That 
reconstructibility is the main contribution. 
The empirical bench supports two claims. The rule engine carries the safety load, since the supervised loop blocks 97.6% 
of adversarial prompts while the unsupervised Proposer blocks none, an asymmetry we expect of an instruction-following 
model. The deterministic check also costs  almost nothing in latency, completing under 10 ms per round against an LLM 
round-trip that dominates the total. Again, compliance is not the bottleneck. 
The argument generalizes beyond finance. The supervisory gap identified in §1 is unlikely to close thr ough model 
advancement alone. It closes when the agent that proposes is structurally distinct from the agent that decides, and when 
the agent that decides is not a language model at all. The decoupling principle independently formalized in [P1] reaches 
the same conclusion through a different route, which we read as evidence that the principle is

the same conclusion through a different route, which we read as evidence that the principle is general rather than specific 
to the financial industry. A practitioner deploying agentic systems in any domain governed by codified rules would benefit 
from the same design choice. 
Three directions look most promising. 
The clearest direction is closing the parameter-learning loop. The framework exposes the institution-tunable parameters 
catalogued in Table 3, with operational defaults shipped in the reference implementation. Three principled tuning 
procedures are available without changing the framework’s structure, namely 𝜔 from enforcement history, 𝜆 from the 
distribution of trade sizes that historically required escalation, and the gate thresholds from precision -recall analysis on 
labeled trades. What is missing across the industry is the infrastructure to log, label, and feed back outcomes fast enough 
to learn from them. Confirmed labels are scarce and arrive late, so these parameters are still chosen rather than learned

Every new adversarial pattern caught in production, and ev ery legitimate request that drew a false block, becomes a

The second direction is expanding rule coverage in breadth  and depth. Breadth means more rules in the existing 
jurisdictions and full international frameworks such as MiFID II, Basel III, and the emerging EU AI Act. Depth means finer-
grained clauses within each rule, including the exception language we now treat as a single trigger. ComplianceNLP [P4]

This research emphasizes the importance of s electing suitable Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning  (RL) architectures 
capable of learning coordinated swarm strategies, exploiting inter-agent dependencies, scaling effectively under dynamic 
and observable fire environments as well as  supporting decentralized exec ution with centralized training. Such 
architectures are essential for enabling emergent cooperation among drones in complex disaster response scenarios. 
4.1. The importance of selecting suitable Multi-Agent RL architectures  
The importance of selecting suitable Mul ti-Agent RL architectures for constructing A gentic AI-driven swarm drones for 
adaptive fire disaster control and prediction cannot be overemphasized. Appropriate architectural selection determines 
not only the learning stability  and con vergence behavior of the system  but it also delineates the extent to which 
autonomous agents can develop coordinated strategies in highly dynamic and partially observable wildfire environments. 
Knowledge of suitable architectural compositions can guide engineers in the timely

Knowledge of suitable architectural compositions can guide engineers in the timely design and deployment of effective 
solutions that can balance deployment deadline, real-time responsiveness, scalability  and efficient coordination of

Practically, differ ent RL architectures encode different assumptions about agent i nteraction, information sharing  and 
policy optimization. For this reason , the choice between v alue-decomposition approaches, single-agent methods and 
centralized training with decentralized execution frameworks directly influences swarm adaptability and operational 
robustness. Well -informed architectural selection enables software engineers to align algorithmic capabilities with

seamlessly from simulation environments t o real -world disaster scenarios  during

electing a suitable architecture plays a critical role in ensuring that learned policies generalize effectively and

Reinforcement learning (RL) in disaster management applications can enable intelligent agents to learn optimal policies 
and deliver efficient mission -critical services. S everal RL architectures have demonstrated potential for autonomous 
disaster management but each of them offer distinct advantages and limitations.  This chapters critically examines the 
suitability of the following RL architectures for designing Agentic AI fire disaster management applications:  
Deep Q-Network (DQN) 
Deep Q -Networks (DQN) combine Q -learning with Deep Neural N etworks to approximate action-value functions in 
complex environments. DQN can be utilized to enable autonomous drones to learn navigation policies, identify high-risk 
fire zones and determine appropriate suppression actions based on environmental observations. The primary strength of 
DQN lies in its ability to learn effective decision policies from high-dimensional state representations without necessarily 
requiring explicit environmental models.

DQN is relatively simple to implement and has demonstrated strong performance in d iscrete dec ision-making tasks. 
However, it  is primarily designed for discrete action spaces and not for  continuous control problems that are often 
encountered in drone operations. Furthermore, the performance of DQN may deteriorate in highly dynamic multi-agent 
environments due to instability and limited scalability. 
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) 
Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is a policy-gradient reinforcement learning algorithm. It is designed to improve on the 
training stability issues associated with the DQN through constrained policy updates. PPO can support adaptive drone 
navigation, fire containment planning  and resource allocation under uncertain environmental conditions  in the above 
settings [13]. 
A major advantage of PPO is its st able learning process. PPO also has the c apability to handle continuous action spaces 
effectively. It has demonstrated strong performance in robotics, autonomous navigation  and complex control tasks.

adaptive route plan ning, real -time decision -making and dynamic suppression strategy selection  in varying fire

7. Ethics, Safety and Governance of Agentic Autonomous Systems 
The above findings point out that the deployment of agentic AI-driven swarm drone system for wildfire suppression and 
disaster response introduces a multidimensional set of constraints that extend beyond algorithmic performance. Although 
these systems demonstrate strong potential for scalable coordination, rapid response and adaptive decision-making, their 
real-world adoption depends on careful consideration of regulatory compliance, best practices, ethical responsibility and 
operational feasibility. Bridging the gap between simulation environments and field deployment therefore requires not 
only technical robustness but also alignment with legal frameworks, safety expectations  and mission-critical reliability 
standards. 
From a regulatory standpoint, agentic AI-driven swarm drone operations must conform to established unmanned aerial 
system (UAS) guidelines. Wildfire disasters and their devastating impacts are global concerns. Therefore, there should be 
strong legislative requirements to govern airspace usage, autonomous flight permissions and safety assurance 
requirements across the glob

This chapter evaluates  the following reinforcement learning approaches: DQN, PPO, A2C, MADDPG, MAPPO and

Artificial Intelligence is entering a new era in which systems are no longer limited to generating predictions or assisting users with isolated tasks. 
Agentic AI represents this transformation by enabling intelligent systems to perceive their environments, reason over complex objectives, plan multi-
step actions, utilize external tools, collaborate with humans and other agents, and continuously adapt to changing conditions. As autonomous 
capabilities mature, Agentic AI is rapidly becoming one of the defining research and application areas of contemporary artificial intelligence.
This edited volume, Agentic AI in the Age of Autonomy with Concepts and Case Studies, has been prepared to provide a comprehensive perspective 
on this emerging paradigm. Rather than focusing solely on technical advances, the book brings together interdisciplinary contributions that examine 
the architectural foundations of agentic systems, human-agent collaboration, governance, domain-specific applications, and future research 
directions. The diversity of the chapters reflects our belief

also by responsible design, societal acceptance, and practical deployment across different sectors.
The book begins by establishing the technical foundations of Agentic AI, explaining the layered architectures, reasoning mechanisms, orchestration 
strategies, and collaborative models that enable autonomous intelligent systems. It then explores issues of trust, governance, ethical responsibility, 
and social acceptance, highlighting the importance of balancing autonomy with transparency, accountability, and human oversight.
Building upon these conceptual foundations, the following chapters examine how autonomous AI agents are transforming software engineering 
from passive development tools into collaborative teammates, while also reviewing the growing role of AI agents in education through current 
architectures, opportunities, and pedagogical challenges. The educational perspective is further ext

The volume continues with practical case studies illustrating the adoption of Agentic AI across diverse application domains. These include intelligent 
destination management supported by tourism dashboards, the interpretation of radiological images through large language models as decision-
support systems in healthcare, neuro-symbolic autonomous governance for financial execution, and the coordination of autonomous swarm drones 
for adaptive wildfire prediction and disaster response. Together, these chapters demonstrate that Agentic AI is evolving beyond a theoretical concept 
into a versatile technological paradigm capable of addressing complex real-world challenges.
